newsitem.title: INDIA: Namibia, India want to revive Non-Aligned Movement.
newsitem.headline: Namibia, India want to revive Non-Aligned Movement.

text.p: Namibia and India called on Friday for a revival of the Non-Aligned Movement of developing countries that lost momentum after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

President Sam Nujoma started a four-day visit to India with a call to breathe new life into the movement and received support from Indian President Shankar Dayal Sharma, who said it was time to revive the 112-nation grouping.
"We want to revive the Non-Aligned Movement in a much more meaningful manner," Nujoma told reporters after a ceremonial reception by the Indian President.
Nujoma also urged Indian firms to boost cooperation between developing countries by investing in Namibia.
The Non-Aligned Movement was originally organised to promote solidarity among newly independent nations and non-alignment from any superpower.
The group has been criticised for having outlived its usefulness after the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.

But its leading members, including India, say the group retains its significance as a symbol of developing countries' solidarity in staying clear of superpower politics and pursuing economic progress.
"The movement of the non-aligned countries has been a vehicle to promote the cause of the liberation of the oppressed people all over the world, and in Namibia in particular," said Nujoma.
Namibia became independent in 1990 after the withdrawal of troops sent by the then apartheid rulers of South Africa. The Non-Aligned Movement had actively lobbied for the withdrawal of troops.
South Africa had said its troops were sent to counter the presence of Cuban troops in Angola.
Cubas presence in the Non-Aligned Movement was a cause for criticism in Western nations, which saw Havana as an Eastern bloc ally.

At a banquet in Nujomas honour, Indian President Sharma said he expected Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) foreign ministers at a meeting in New Delhi this year to consider measures to strengthen the movement.

"Together, we have to build and revivify the Non-Aligned Movement, as an instrument of promoting peace, disarmament and development and to build a more just world order, two-thirds of which is represented by the members of the NAM," Sharma said.
Earlier, Nujoma told a business luncheon that Windhoek was keen to attract Indian investors to boost small industries that had mushroomed since independence.
"Namibia is open for business. What we lack is capital and expertise," Nujoma said.

Agriculture Minister Helmut Angula, who is accompanying Nujoma, told the meeting that Namibia aimed to boost agricultural and livestock exports to Asia, and asked for foreign expertise to develop these businesses.
